etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Borrowed from Latin ēlēctus, past participle of ēligō (“to pick out, choose, elect”), from ē- (“out”) + legō (“to pick out, pick, gather, collect, etc.”); see legend.

Cognate to eclectic, which is via Ancient Greek rather than Latin, hence prefix ἐκ (ek), rather than e- (from ex).

definitions.definition: (theology) In Calvinist theology, one foreordained to Heaven. In other Christian theologies, someone chosen by God for salvation.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 42:1:
quote.text: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 18:7:
quote.text: Shall not God avenge his won elect?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To choose or make a decision (to do something)
(transitive) To choose (a candidate) in an election
(postpositive) Who has been elected in a specified post, but has not yet entered office.

quote.citation: 1811, Jane Austen, chapter 16, in Sense and Sensibility:
quote.text: She began almost to feel a dislike of Edward; and it ended, as every feeling must end with her, by carrying back her thoughts to Willoughby, whose manners formed a contrast sufficiently striking to those of his brother elect.

definitions.definition: Chosen; taken by preference from among two or more.
